# Publishing That Rebuilds Itself {#sec-quarto}



Most reports are built by hand. An analyst runs a script, copies a number into a Word
document, pastes a chart into a slide, retypes the same number in an email, and exports a
PDF for the website. Every copy is a small act of faith that the number was right and is
still right. When the data change, someone has to find every copy, and nobody can say for
sure where each one came from.

This chapter is about the alternative this book teaches: **one source that rebuilds every
output**. It explains what Quarto is and what happens when it renders a document, why it is
deliberately not an AI tool even though this book uses one alongside it, and what
"reproducible" does and does not promise. It ends with the cases where Quarto is the wrong
choice, because a tool you cannot argue against is a tool you do not understand yet.

## Why reports drift {#sec-drift}

The London visitor guide that runs through Part II is a small example of a common problem.
The tourism office publishes the same facts to several audiences: a web guide for
visitors, a dashboard for managers, a Word brief for partners, a printed flyer, and later
a white paper. In the finished project, 5 pages read the same table of
attraction visits, and between them they write 10 files: the guide alone
becomes a web page, a Word document, a PDF, a PowerPoint deck, an e-book and a set of
slides.

Suppose the Association of Leading Visitor Attractions (ALVA), the source of those counts,
corrects one figure. In a copy-and-paste workflow, that correction has to reach
10 files by hand. Three things tend to go wrong:

- **Stale numbers.** One copy is missed, and the flyer disagrees with the dashboard.
- **Lost provenance.** Six months later, nobody can say which version of the data
  produced the number in the partner brief.
- **Slow change.** Because every update is expensive, updates stop happening, and the
  documents quietly age.

None of these is a failure of care. They are what happens when the *output* is treated as
the thing you edit. The fix is structural: edit the source, and let a program rebuild the
outputs.

## What Quarto is {#sec-what-quarto}

Quarto is an open-source publishing system: a command-line program that turns plain-text
source files into finished documents. It is free for anyone to use; the Quarto command-line
tool has been under the MIT License since version 1.4 (GNU GPL v2 before that), and the
tools it bundles have their own open-source licences (Quarto licence page, checked
2026-11-06).

The input is either a plain Markdown file (`.md`) or a Quarto document (`.qmd`). A `.qmd`
file is Markdown with two additions: a block of settings at the top, written in YAML, and
*code cells*, fenced blocks of code that run when the document is built. Here is a complete
one, the file the test run in @sec-setup asks your assistant to write:

````markdown
---
title: "Hello"
format:
  html: default
  typst: default
---

```{{python}}
answer = 6 * 7
```

The answer is `{{python}} answer`.
````

The sentence at the bottom contains *inline code*: when the document is built, Quarto runs
`answer` and writes its value into the sentence. When this book was built, the same
calculation gave 42, and that number was computed, not typed.

### Three steps: execute, convert, typeset

`quarto render` does three things in order (@fig-pipeline).

![What `quarto render` does. One source becomes Markdown with results, which Pandoc converts to each output format; for PDF, Typst typesets the result.](../media/diagrams/render-pipeline){#fig-pipeline .on-light fig-alt="A source file, london.qmd, holding Markdown, YAML and code cells, goes through three steps. Step 1, execute: Jupyter for Python or knitr for R runs each code cell. The result is Markdown with the results in place of the code. Step 2, convert: Pandoc turns that Markdown into html, docx, epub, pptx and revealjs. Step 3, typeset: for PDF, Pandoc writes Typst source and Typst typesets it into a pdf. One command, quarto render, runs all three steps."}

1. **Execute.** A computation engine runs the code cells. For Python, that engine is
   Jupyter; for R, it is knitr. Quarto's other principal languages are Julia and Observable
   JavaScript, which runs in the reader's browser, and Jupyter kernels add many more. The
   results (numbers, tables, figures) replace the code in an intermediate Markdown file.
   This book uses Python only.
2. **Convert.** Pandoc, a long-established document converter, reads that Markdown once and
   writes each requested format: HTML, Word (`docx`), EPUB, PowerPoint (`pptx`) or a
   Reveal.js slide deck.
3. **Typeset.** For PDF, Pandoc writes source for Typst, a modern typesetting system that
   ships inside Quarto, and Typst produces the PDF. No LaTeX installation is needed. (Quarto
   can also make PDFs through LaTeX, `format: pdf`, if you install a TeX distribution.)

The split matters in practice. A failure in step 1 is a failure of *your code*: a missing
package, a wrong column name, a cell that raises an error. A failure in step 2 or 3 is a
failure of *the document*: a malformed table, an image too large for the page, a
format-specific option that does not exist. When a render fails, the error message tells
you which step stopped, and that tells you where to look.

::: why
Pandoc converts between many formats by reading every input into one internal document
model and writing every output from that model. That is why one Markdown file can become
both a Word document and a slide deck: neither output is derived from the other. Both come
from the same structured intermediate, so a heading is a heading everywhere.
:::

### What comes out

The official list of formats is long and grouped by kind (Quarto, *All Formats*, checked
2026-10-30):

| Kind | Formats used in this book | Others |
|---|---|---|
| Documents | HTML, PDF (Typst), Word, EPUB | OpenDocument, PDF through LaTeX |
| Presentations | Reveal.js, PowerPoint | Beamer |
| The web | websites, blogs, dashboards | |
| More | | Markdown variants, Jupyter notebooks, JATS, wikis |

: Quarto's output formats, as grouped in the official list. {#tbl-formats}

Websites, blogs and dashboards are built from the same `.qmd` files; what changes is a
project setting, not the content. Part II builds all of them from one London guide, and
Part III builds a report, slides, a blog post and a website from one water analysis.

## Quarto is not AI {#sec-not-ai}

This book pairs Quarto with a coding assistant, and the pairing invites a misunderstanding:
that Quarto itself is an AI tool. It is not. Quarto is conventional software. Given the
same source files and the same data, it writes the same outputs every time. It does not
generate text, code or figures of its own, and it sends nothing to an AI service.

The assistant is a separate program. It reads and writes the files in your project folder
and runs commands you approve; Quarto then turns those files into formats. The two have
different failure modes, and the workflow in this book is designed around the difference:

| | Coding assistant | Quarto |
|---|---|---|
| Output for the same input | varies from run to run | identical |
| Typical mistake | plausible but wrong code or prose | a precise, reproducible error |
| How you check it | read its changes, run them, compare with the data | read the rendered output |

: Two tools with different failure modes. {#tbl-split}

Because generation and rendering are separate, every mistake the assistant makes lands in
a file you can read before anything is published. And because the render is repeatable,
anyone can rebuild your outputs to confirm them, without trusting the assistant at all.

::: pitfall
Quarto runs whatever code your cells contain. If a cell calls an AI service, the document
becomes as unpredictable as that service, and the cause is your code, not Quarto. Keep
calls to models out of rendered documents unless the variation is the point.
:::

## Reproducible: same source, same result {#sec-reproducible}

*Reproducible* is used loosely, so here is the precise sense this book means: someone else,
or you in six months, can rebuild the same results from the same files with one command,
and can see where every number came from. Four properties make that possible:

**One source.** Text, code and data live in plain files in one folder. Nothing important
exists only inside an application.

**Numbers are computed.** Every figure, table and number in a sentence comes from a code
cell or inline code that reads the data. Nothing is typed in or pasted from elsewhere.

**One command.** `quarto render` rebuilds everything. There is no sequence of manual
export steps to remember.

**Versioned.** Git, the version-control tool installed in @sec-setup, records each saved
state of the source, data and settings as a *commit* with a message saying why it changed.
Any earlier state can be restored, two states can be compared, and a result can be tied to
the exact files that made it. The project's Python packages are pinned too, in a lockfile
(`uv.lock`, introduced in @sec-markdown), so a colleague's machine builds the same
environment as yours.

Together these turn the drift problem around. Correct one value in the data, render, and
the table, the chart and the sentence that quote it all update together, in every format.

::: practice
**Pause and think.** You correct one number in the data. What do you retype in the report?

Nothing. You fix the data file and render again. If the answer is anything else, some
number in the report was typed rather than computed, and that is the bug to fix.
:::

::: pitfall
Reproducible does not mean correct. A wrong analysis reproduces perfectly: the same wrong
number appears in every format, every time. Reproducibility makes errors *findable*,
because anyone can trace a number back to its code and data, but you still have to check
results against their sources. @sec-causation is an extended example of a result that
reproduces cleanly and still must not be read the way it first appears.
:::

There is one more subtlety, which matters once projects grow. Rendering every page from
scratch can be slow, so Quarto can cache results with a setting called `freeze`. A cache
is only as good as its rule for throwing results away, and Quarto re-executes a frozen page
when *that page's source* changes, not when a data file it reads changes. @sec-publish-many
shows how to use the cache safely. This book itself uses one, with a documented way to
clear it (@sec-how-built).

## When Quarto is the wrong tool {#sec-wrong-tool}

Quarto earns its keep when the same content is rebuilt, either because the data change or
because the content goes to several audiences. It costs you a plain-text workflow, a
command line and some setup. That trade is not always worth making:

- **Collaborators who edit in Word.** If the people who revise the document work in a word
  processor with tracked changes, they can comment on the Word output, but their edits have
  to be carried back into the source by hand. For documents whose main work is
  multi-author line editing, a shared word processor may simply fit better.
- **Designed layouts.** Quarto produces structured documents: headings, paragraphs,
  figures, tables. Typst and CSS can take the look a long way, but a poster or a
  brand-heavy brochure laid out to the millimetre is easier in a design tool.
- **Format fidelity at the edges.** Each format can only carry what it supports. Pandoc
  writes good Word and PowerPoint files, but a PowerPoint table cannot hold pictures, for
  example, so the London guide's photo table shows each photo's alt text in its `pptx`
  version instead. Check every format you promise to deliver.
- **One-off documents.** A two-paragraph note with no data and no second audience gains
  little from a build system.

::: practice
A useful test: will this document be built a second time? If the data will change, if a
second audience will need it in another format, or if someone will ask "where did this
number come from?", the plain-text workflow pays for itself quickly. If none of these is
likely, use whatever is fastest.
:::

## Summary {.unnumbered}

Reports drift because their outputs are edited by hand. Quarto removes the copies: a `.qmd`
source holds text, settings and code; `quarto render` executes the code, converts the
result with Pandoc and, for PDF, typesets it with Typst. Quarto is deterministic software,
separate from the coding assistant that writes its sources, and that separation is what
makes an assistant's mistakes inspectable. Reproducibility rests on one source, computed
numbers, one command and version control; it makes results checkable, not automatically
right. Use Quarto when a document will be rebuilt, and something simpler when it will not.
